take: The Brent-WTI spread blowing out to $12 is the story that matters most today, because it tells you the market is pricing Hormuz tail risk and diesel scarcity into the waterborne crude complex whilst landlocked US barrels sit behind a freight and export bottleneck. The second theme is the diesel export threat: Trump backing a halt to US diesel exports has Britain on edge, and with Houston crude tanker bunker operations already dropping this month, any export restriction would hit product tanker tonne-miles and European distillate supply simultaneously. On positioning, the EIA has US crude output averaging 13.8m b/d in 2026, a fresh record, and the rig count ticked up again this week, so the fundamental backdrop is lengthening supply even as the paper market pays up for geopolitical optionality. The cross-market link to watch is gasoil versus bunker: elevated crack spreads are already feeding pump prices, and if the diesel export ban gains traction, European gasoil tightness will pull VLSFO and marine fuel higher in sympathy, squeezing shipowners already facing a resilience premium. In the next 24 hours, watch whether the US-Iran truce talk actually reopens Hormuz within the week, because if it does, that $12 Brent-WTI spread unwinds fast and the diesel fear trade deflates with it.

items.title: Henry Hub natural gas prices this summer were 6% lower than last summer
items.summary: The Henry Hub natural gas spot price averaged $2.93 per million British thermal units from June through August, 6% less than the same period last year. Prices were lower this summer despite exceptionally hot weather that increased electricity demand for air conditioning. Natural gas-fired power plants often help meet higher demand during such periods.

items.title: Public companies produce most U.S. crude oil and natural gas
items.summary: Publicly traded companies represent a tiny share of the total number of companies producing crude oil and natural gas in the United States, but they make up a large share of U.S. production. In 2025, publicly traded companies accounted for just 2% of about 12,000 oil and natural gas producers but produced 68% of the crude oil and natural gas in the Lower 48 states.

items.title: What goes into diesel prices?
items.summary: The price of distillate fuel oil, often sold as diesel, is driven by the price of crude oil, retail margins, distribution costs, taxes, and crack spreads, the indicator we use for refining margins. Tight global supplies of distillate fuel oil and elevated crude oil prices have driven prices higher in recent months.
